sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A light-emitting diode is a forward-biased pn junction designed so that injected electrons and holes recombine by emitting **photons**. Each such radiative event releases about one band gap of energy, so the band gap sets the colour.

Not every semiconductor can do this efficiently. In a **direct-gap** material (GaAs, InP, GaN), the lowest conduction-band state and the highest valence-band state have the same crystal momentum \(k\), so an electron can drop straight down and emit a photon. In an **indirect-gap** material such as silicon they are offset in \(k\); a photon carries almost no momentum, so a phonon must also take part. That is rare, and most recombination goes through traps and makes heat instead. That is why LEDs are made from III-V compounds, while silicon is fine for absorbing light in solar cells and photodetectors. A lens on top collects the light and directs it.
sections.figure_alt: Direct band gap E-k diagram: the conduction-band minimum sits directly above the valence-band maximum, so a vertical (photon-only) transition connects them.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Photon energy and wavelength:
\[ E_g = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}, \qquad \lambda\,(\mu\mathrm{m}) = \frac{1.24}{E_g\,(\mathrm{eV})} \]
Photon rate from current \(I\) with internal efficiency \(\eta\): \(\dot N = \eta I/q\).
Optical power: \(P \approx \dot N E_g = \eta\,I\,E_g/q\).
sections.figure_alt: Indirect band gap E-k diagram: the conduction-band minimum is offset in k from the valence-band maximum, so a transition needs a phonon as well as a photon.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A GaN-based LED with \(E_g = 3.1\ \mathrm{eV}\):
\[ \lambda = \frac{1.24}{3.1} = 0.40\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 400\ \mathrm{nm} \]
That is violet. Driven at 15 mA with 40% of the injected carriers emitting photons:
\[ \dot N = \frac{0.4 \times 0.015}{1.602\times10^{-19}} \approx 3.7\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}, \qquad P \approx 0.4 \times 15\ \mathrm{mA} \times 3.1\ \mathrm{V} \approx 18.6\ \mathrm{mW} \]

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Thinking the LED colour depends on the current. It is set by \(E_g\).
- Using 1.24 with λ in nm; it gives µm.
- Calling 870 nm red; visible light ends near 700 nm.
- Assuming silicon cannot absorb light; it absorbs well, but it rarely emits.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Electrically an LED is just a diode, so its forward voltage and small-signal resistance follow the diode equation. A photodiode (a reverse-biased junction) brings in junction capacitance, which you will see again as a speed limit in transistors.
